markdown_content: ## Sketch On Avatar (Clo 2026.0): Goal and Workflow This section explains what the **Sketching feature** in **Clo 2026.0** is for and how it helps designers iterate quickly. The feature is intended for users who want to start with **sketching/drawing** rather than beginning with a **pattern**. You can sketch directly onto an avatar inside Clo to quickly explore ideas and then hand the result off to downstream work (e.g., **Pattern Maker**, **Tech Designer**, or a **vendor**). The speaker highlights that this reduces the burden on non-pattern-makers by letting them focus on the creative idea first. ### Input Methods: Wacom Tablet or Three-Button Mouse The sketching tool supports: - **Wacom tablet**: recommended; you can sketch on top of the tablet and it works well in Clo. - **Three-button mouse**: also supported; the demo uses a mouse because no tablet is available. ### Where to Find the Tool The sketching tool is located in the **3D toolbar**. After selecting the **sketching tool**, a **sketch box** appears, with drawing controls inside it. --- ## Sketch Tool Controls: Pen, Eraser, Symmetry, and Conversion Guides This section covers the core sketch controls: switching between **pen/eraser**, using **symmetry**, and enabling **conversion guides** to see how strokes become 3D/flat pattern elements. ### Pen and Eraser Inside the sketch box: - A **pen** mode behaves like a pencil for drawing. - An **eraser** mode lets you choose the **eraser size**. - The demo notes that the pen and eraser size options are available within the tool. ### Symmetry A **Symmetry** option adds mirror/another-line behavior to your sketch. When symmetry is enabled, you can connect the resulting lines to help form an outfit shape more quickly. ### Conversion Guides (Previewing 3D-to-Pattern Conversion) Under symmetry, there are **conversion guides** that help show what your **pen lines will become** after conversion. Key related option: - **Convert to 3D pen**: converts the sketch so it can be **flattened** into a more pattern-like representation. If you don’t want to worry about pattern conversion immediately, you can sketch first and convert later. --- ## Viewpoint (Front/Back), Navigation Limits, and Live Updating This section explains how the sketch view works using **viewpoint** (front/back) and what navigation actions are supported (zoom/pan) versus not supported (rotation). It also describes how conversion lines update as you edit. ### Viewpoint Controls: Front and Back The tool includes **viewpoint** settings: - Start with **front** view. - Switch to **back** view to continue drawing on the back side. The demo emphasizes that you can: - **Zoom in and out** - **Pan** But you **cannot rotate** in the current sketching view mode (the speaker mentions attempting to rotate while right-clicking/holding). ### Editing and Automatic Conversion Line Updates After drawing: - You can switch to **eraser** to remove parts that are too close or need adjustment. - You can zoom in to refine details. - As you erase and redraw, the **conversion lines update automatically** to reflect the new sketch geometry. Example adjustments mentioned: - Removing a line that is “too close” - Redrawing so the shape extends outward more - Increasing “back height” by erasing and adjusting - Refining seam-related areas by repeated erase/redraw cycles --- ## Converting to 3D Pen and Flattening: Save, Reopen, and Edit This section explains how to finalize a sketch by using **Convert to 3D pen**, how to **flatten** it, and how to save/reopen the project for further work and editing. ### Convert to 3D Pen and Flatten After sketching and refining: - Turn on **Convert to 3D pen** to transform the sketch into a 3D pen representation. - Then you can **flatten** the result to get a pattern-like output. The speaker notes that conversion does not always produce a perfect result automatically, but it provides a strong starting point that can be edited. ### Save as Project and Continue Later The demo workflow includes: - **File → Save As Project** - Example project naming in the demo: “**fancy dress cocktail**” (used as an example) - Reopen the project later and continue work in Clo The speaker also describes the collaboration flow: - After reopening, you can pass it to a **pattern maker**, **tech designer**, or **vendor** to continue from there. - Alternatively, the recipient can find a similar pattern and build from the sketch-derived starting point. ### Editing After Conversion Once converted: - You can **edit geometry** (e.g., delete lines, move lines, reconnect elements). - The speaker specifically mentions: - **Delete** - **Move** lines - **Connect** segments - The seam areas (especially **side seams**) are described as sometimes the trickiest to get perfect, so editing may be needed. --- ## Using Avatar Pen Tools: Drawing On/Off the Avatar and Point-Based Editing This section covers how the speaker uses avatar pen tools to draw and edit directly relative to the avatar surface, including finishing strokes and adjusting points/circles. ### Drawing On and Off the Avatar The demo uses shortcuts/controls to draw: - Press **P** to toggle **draw on/off the avatar spaces**. - Press **Enter** to **finish** the current drawing action. ### Edit Avatar Pen Tool and Point Editing Then the speaker switches to: - **Edit Avatar Pen Tool** A point-based editing action is described: - **Right-click → add circle around avatar** - The speaker notes the result may not be exactly as desired at first because the sketch may not have been extended far enough, but it can be corrected. ### Adjusting and Flattening Selectively The demo emphasizes flexibility: - You can **move and adjust** the added circle/points. - When flattening, you can choose the side you prefer rather than needing “perfect symmetry” from the start. --- ## Practical Examples: Garments, Symmetry vs No Symmetry, and Quick Iteration This section demonstrates how the sketching workflow supports different garment types (e.g., dresses and tops) using symmetry or without symmetry, then converting and flattening to preview structure. ### Symmetry and Garment Shaping The speaker notes: - If symmetry is enabled, you can rely on it for mirrored construction and reduce redo work. - Side seams may still require attention. ### Off-Shoulder and A-Line / Flowy Dress Ideas (No Symmetry Example) A “no symmetry” approach is presented as useful for designs like: - **Off-shoulder** styles - **A-line** dresses - **Empire waist** / **flowy dress skirt** concepts Workflow shown: 1. Sketch with symmetry turned off (or not using symmetry) 2. **Back → Convert to 3D pen** 3. Flatten to see what the garment will look like without structural pattern-making effort The demo highlights that this helps users understand the garment’s look even if they’re not making a “true pattern.” ### Tack/Clarity Aids to Improve Fit The speaker repeatedly references **tacks** and mentions tools that improve: - **Notice** and **clarity** (as described) - Overall fit adjustments (e.g., making the design fit “a little bit better”) They also mention that tacks and side guidance tools can help refine areas like darts and spacing. ### Multiple Garment Options The speaker lists that the tool supports many garment types, including: - **Dresses** (including off-shoulder variants) - **Sweetheart top** - **Empire waist** with a flowy skirt - “Other items” for business use (general variety) --- ## Limitations and Expectations: Not Perfect Yet, but Fast for Ideation This section clarifies the current limitations and sets expectations about accuracy and editing requirements. The speaker explicitly states: - The feature is **not guaranteed to produce perfect results** immediately. - Some edits are expected (e.g., seams, line spacing, geometry adjustments). - The sketching-to-pattern workflow is still valuable because it lets users: - **Sketch ideas quickly** - **Avoid starting from a pattern** - **Iterate without needing to be a pattern maker** They also note the feature is the **first time** it has been developed in this form and that **improvements are expected along the way**.
